summary: Assigns one of the reserved label values from RFC 3032 as the OAM Alert Label, used to identify user-plane MPLS operation and maintenance packets. This lets routers tell management test packets from ordinary traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3429 picks the number 14 out of the reserved MPLS label values and names it the OAM Alert Label. A router that sees that label on a packet knows the packet is a network test packet and not customer traffic. The document also explains what happens to such a packet when the last router on the path is reached through penultimate hop popping.

questions: how does an mpls router recognise an oam packet
subtitle: The MPLS label that marks a packet as an operation and maintenance test packet

tldr.problem: User-plane MPLS operation and maintenance functions send their own test packets through the network, and a router needs to tell those packets apart from the customer traffic it is carrying.
tldr.mechanism: The document assigns one of the reserved label values from the MPLS label stack encoding to the OAM Alert Label. The value 14 is used, and the ITU-T Y.1711 mechanisms put it on top of the OAM packet so the receiving node knows what it has been sent.
tldr.outcome: The assignment lets the Y.1711 OAM mechanisms be carried over MPLS networks, including the case where the penultimate node pops the top label before the packet reaches the node that started the test.

today: RFC 3429 is an Informational memo published in November 2002, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The value it assigns, label 14, is the value that identifies user-plane MPLS OAM packets in the ITU-T Y.1711 mechanisms the document describes.

sections.title: What the Document Assigns
sections.content:
RFC 3429 describes the assignment of one of the reserved label values defined in RFC 3032, the MPLS label stack encoding, to the OAM Alert Label. The label is used by the user-plane Multiprotocol Label Switching operation and maintenance functions to identify MPLS OAM packets, in the way described by ITU-T Recommendation Y.1711 on MPLS OAM functions.

The document is short and factual. It explains what the MPLS OAM functions are for, records the assignment of the label value, notes the related work in ITU-T Study Group 13, and answers the questions that were raised about how the OAM packets behave when penultimate hop popping is in effect.
sections.plainLanguage: This document gives a reserved MPLS label a name and a value. Routers use that label to recognise a network test packet so they do not treat it as customer traffic.

sections.title: What the OAM Functions Do
sections.content:
MPLS OAM functions give network operators the tools to operate and maintain their networks. The functionality is required at the MPLS layer, and more specifically at each MPLS level, independent of the OAM functionality provided by lower layers such as SONET/SDH. The objectives are four.

  • Defect and failure detection. Defects and failures that affect the transport of user information are detected by continuous or periodic checking, and maintenance event information or appropriate alarms are produced as a result.
  • Reporting the defect and failure information. The information is given to other management entities, such as an Operation Support System, so that maintenance staff get the indications they need to maintain the Quality of Service level offered to customers.
  • Defect and failure localisation. Determination by internal or external test systems of a failed entity is performed when the defect information is not sufficient.
  • Performance monitoring. The performance of the user information transport, including packet losses, transfer delay and bit errors, is measured so that the integrity of the transport can be estimated.
sections.plainLanguage: The OAM functions are the network's own checks: they spot faults, report them to the operator, find which piece of equipment failed, and measure how well traffic is being carried.

sections.title: The OAM Alert Label
sections.content:
The user-plane MPLS OAM mechanisms described in ITU-T Recommendation Y.1711 use a special label, the OAM Alert Label, to tell OAM packets apart from normal user packets. One of the reserved label values defined in the MPLS label stack encoding is assigned to it, and the value used is 14.

The IANA has reserved the use of the MPLS label value 14 as the OAM Alert Label. The document also lists the related ITU-T Study Group 13 Question 3/13 documents: Recommendation Y.1710 on the requirements for OAM functionality for MPLS networks, Corrigendum 1 to Y.1710, Recommendation Y.1711 on OAM mechanisms for MPLS networks, and Draft Recommendation Y.1720 on protection switching for MPLS networks, which relies on the mechanisms in Y.1711 and was under last call as of November 2002.
sections.plainLanguage: The label value 14 is the marker. A router that pops the top label and sees 14 underneath knows the packet is an OAM test packet, not customer traffic.

sections.title: Node Behaviour with Penultimate Hop Popping
sections.content:
Penultimate hop popping, or PHP, is where the node before the destination removes the top label from the label stack instead of swapping it. There are two cases. In the first, the ultimate node is an MPLS Label Switching Router that implements both the control plane and the data plane but cannot perform two lookups at line rate, so it asks the penultimate node to pop the top label, using the MPLS reserved label 3, the implicit null label. In the second, the ultimate node has no MPLS label look-up or processing capability at all and does not recognise labelled packets, so it also asks for PHP using the implicit null label.

At present the MPLS OAM functions defined in Y.1711 can only be applied to the first case. Application to the second case needs further study, and application to carrier supporting carrier scenarios is for future study.

Where the ultimate node is an MPLS LSR and PHP is in effect, the penultimate node pops the top label and forwards the OAM packet, with the OAM label and the OAM payload intact, to the ultimate node. If that node supports MPLS OAM, it understands that the packet it received with an OAM label on top is an OAM packet, since the original top label was removed by the penultimate node. It also knows which node started the OAM packet, from the TTSI, the Trail Termination Source Identifier, value carried in the packet. If the ultimate node does not support MPLS OAM, the OAM packet is discarded, as specified in section 3.18 of RFC 3031.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the router before the destination removes the top label instead of forwarding it. The OAM packet then arrives with the alert label on top, so the destination router knows it is a test packet and knows which node sent it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document does not raise any security issues that are not already present in either the MPLS architecture or in the architecture of the network layer protocol contained within the encapsulation.

It adds that OAM functions could enhance the security of MPLS networks. The Connectivity Verification function defined in ITU-T Recommendation Y.1711 can detect mis-connections, and therefore can prevent customers' traffic being exposed to other customers.
sections.plainLanguage: The label assignment adds no new security risk. The document notes one benefit: a connectivity check can spot a wrongly connected path and stop one customer's traffic reaching another customer.
